new_statements.translation: 5. Stress and tones. All Chatino words are pronounced with greatest force on the last syllable. Since this is a general rule, it is not necessary to write the accent. [...] In this dictionary the tone of the last syllable of each word is indicated by a superscript number after the headword. [p. 352:] Besides the general intonation of a sentence, every Chatino word carries a special tone on the last syllable, the stressed syllable. [...] In pretonic syllables the only tones that occur are low, 4, and high, 2

El acento y los tonos': 'Todas las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba. (2) p. 352 = PDF p. 377, 'Gramática chatina'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the (native) word, which is also the tone-bearing syllable; earlier syllables are pretonic and carry only reduced tonal contrasts. Sullivant 2015 (pp. 54-55) restates this for all Core Chatino incl. every Eastern Chatino topolect as stem-final stress (word-final unless enclitics follow).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. Pride & Pride p. 348: in trisyllabic compounds (e.g. jakatunʔ 'tamal' < tyaja + katunʔ) the first syllable 'sigue llevando un poco del acento original' and the word is pronounced like a two-word phrase; Spanish loans of more than two syllables split into two phonological words.
new_statements.exceptions: Nasal and long vowels occur only in the final syllable 'con la excepción de algunas palabras de origen español' (p. 348); loans with medial clusters (lomstan 'limosna') behave as two phonological words. Sullivant: stress is stem-final, so enclitics fall outside the stressed syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (native words are mono- or disyllabic, final syllable stressed); tone statements refer to words in isolation as dictionary headwords. The grammar reflects Panixtlahuaca speech but the authors state it 'se puede aplicar a toda la zona alta en general' (p. ix); cly (Lachao, Yolotepec) forms appear only as lexical variants.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog east2558 = ISO [cly] 'Eastern Highland Chatino' = Ethnologue's Lachao-Yolotepec group (San Juan Lachao Nuevo/Viejo, Santa María Yolotepec; Pride & Pride's 'sierra oriental'), NOT Woodbury's broad 'Eastern Chatino' (east2736), and not SJQ/Yaitepec/Panixtlahuaca (those are [ctp] west2644 in Glottolog). Campbell 2013 and Cruz & Woodbury 2014 reject cly as a genetic unit within Eastern Chatino. The quoted statement is from Pride & Pride's dictionary of 'chatino de la zona alta', whose grammar 'refleja más bien el habla de la gente de Panixtlahuaca' (ctp, pani1261/west2644) but which the authors say applies to the whole zona alta and which includes Lach. and Yol. lexical variants; corroborated second-hand by Sullivant 2015:55 for 'all extant topolects of Eastern Chatino'. No stress statement based specifically on Lachao or Yolotepec data was found.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress section: the talks are about tone inventories and tone sequences. Prominence is mentioned only in passing: in Zacatepec the final mora is 'the prominent mora of the word', and the majority of Eastern Chatino varieties (SJQ etc.) lost their non-prominent, i.e. non-final, vowels. So word prominence is final (last mora/syllable) and non-final syllables are weak enough to have been lost in most Eastern Chatino.

new_statements.quote: [PDF p. 2] "Por regular una palabra fonológica en chatino de Panixtlahuaca consta de una o dos sílabas, aunque tres sílabas pueden aparecer al nivel fonético debido a una regla de silabización de consonantes, discutida en sección 4. La última sílaba de la palabra lleva el acento. En la sílaba tónica contrastan todas las consonantes, todas las vocales, y todos los tonos. Al contraste, en la sílaba átona, no se encuentran las vocales largas, ni las vocales nasalizadas, y sólo se encuentran cuatro tonos contrastantes." [PDF p. 24] "cada palabra chatina lleva un tono especial en su última sílaba, la sílaba acentuada."
new_statements.translation: 'Normally a phonological word in Panixtlahuaca Chatino consists of one or two syllables, although three syllables can appear at the phonetic level because of a consonant-syllabification rule discussed in section 4. The last syllable of the word carries the stress. In the stressed syllable all the consonants, all the vowels and all the tones contrast. By contrast, in the unstressed syllable neither long vowels nor nasalized vowels are found, and only four contrasting tones are found.' [p. 24] 'each Chatino word carries a special tone on its last syllable, the stressed syllable.'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress) and the existing Pride & Pride 2004 statement 'Todas las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba'. It is the phonological write-up behind that dictionary, by the same author, and adds the detail that final = full-contrast syllable, non-final = reduced contrasts, plus the loanword repairs. Caveat: it explicitly describes 'el hablar de San Miguel Panixtlahuaca' [ctp], the same base variety as the catalog's source dictionary, not Lachao or Yolotepec themselves.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the last syllable of every phonological word (words are at most disyllabic apart from a few compounds). The stressed final syllable carries the full contrasts (all consonants, vowels, eight tones); the unstressed syllable allows no long or nasalized vowels and only low (4) vs high (2) tone. At phrase level the last stress of the phonological phrase is the strongest.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not for native words. In sec. 8 (PDF p. 38) Spanish loans with non-final stress are handled by (i) splitting them into two phonological words, each stressed, 'pero la última tiene el mayor acento. Esto resulta de la regla que hace más fuerte el último acento de la frase fonológica'; (ii) dropping the other syllables (mba 'compadre', mstru 'maestro'); or (iii) moving the stress to the end (kuta 'vaca', kulo: 'color').
new_statements.exceptions: Only Spanish loans, which are reshaped to fit the final-stress pattern (see secondary_stress). Certain common homographs are written with an acute accent to mark the higher tone (PDF p. 25), an orthographic device, not a stress difference.

sources.note: Sec. 5 'El acento y los tonos', p. xiii: all Chatino words are pronounced with greatest force on the last syllable; stress need not be. Grammar sketch p. 352: each word carries its tone on the last syllable, 'la sílaba acentuada'; pretonic syllables take only tone 2 or 4. p. 348: in trisyllabic compounds the first syllable keeps a little of its original accent, pronounced as a two-word phrase. Grammar based on Panixtlahuaca [ctp] but stated to apply to the whole zona alta (Eastern Chatino); dictionary gives Lach. and Yol. (cly) variant forms (122 tagged lines).
